OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Determine the appropriate preoperative imaging studies required to evaluate bone loss in
patients in whom primary total hip arthroplasty fails.
Describe the two major classification systems for acetabular and femoral bone loss.
Identify the treatment ramifications of acetabular and femoral bone loss in planning
reconstruction for revision total hip arthroplasty.
Overview

Overview
In evaluating a patient for revision total hip arthroplasty, surgeons must assess the bone
stock that will be available for reconstruction. This is primarily determined via plain

radiographs and three-dimensional imaging studies; however, in performing a two-stage
revision for infection, cataloging bone loss and remaining bone stock is possible during
the first stage. On the acetabular side, bone loss ranges from minor areas that can be
reconstructed with the use of a hemispherical acetabular component to pelvic
discontinuity that requires adjunct fixation with the use of a cage or a custom triflange
component. Similarly, minor bone loss in the femur can be managed with the use of a
primary press fit or cemented stem, whereas extensive metaphyseal and diaphyseal
bone loss may necessitate a tapered distal fitting stem or even proximal femur
replacement. Surgeons should understand the evaluation of acetabular and femoral
bone loss and the ramifications for reconstruction in revision total hip arthroplasty.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs should be obtained in perpendicular planes.
Acetabular osteolysis is characterized by size and location (DeLee and Charnley classification
system).1
Zone 1 (superolateral), zone 2 (central), and zone 3 (inferomedial)
Plain radiographs may underestimate the severity of the osteolysis.
Ancillary radiographs (Judet views) or CT scans may aid in additional assessment of bone
available for reconstruction.
Femoral osteolysis is characterized by size and location (Gruen classification system).2
Zones 1 through 7: progressing from proximal/lateral greater trochanter, distally to the tip
of the implant and back up the medial side to the lesser trochanter

Radiography
An AP radiograph of the pelvis should allow for visualization of the contralateral hip. This
is vital in preoperative planning and templating to assess for leg-length inequality and
normal femoral and acetabular morphology. If concern for acetabular bone loss exists,
Judet radiographs should be obtained to assess bone stock on the acetabular side and

the integrity of the anterior and posterior columns. These views allow for an initial
evaluation of bone loss and may demonstrate pelvic discontinuity.
Thin-cut CT scans routinely are obtained to allow for a more detailed evaluation of the
remaining bone stock available for acetabular reconstruction.
Computed Tomography
CT enables assessment of the size and location of bone loss.
The quality and location of the remaining bone can be better determined.
CT also is useful for creating models for reconstruction or customized implants.

Computed Tomography
In addition to Judet radiographs, CT scans are helpful in patients with considerable
acetabular bone loss. Surgeons must understand the amount of bone remaining and the
location of the bone to determine if a hemispheric acetabular component will likely
achieve an adequate pinch fit between the anterosuperior bone of the anterior column
and the posteroinferior bone of the posterior column. If this bone is questionable, a
three-dimensional model can be created to provide additional detail.


Acetabulum
The Paprosky classification of acetabular bone loss is most widely used and considers
four radiographic variables (Resource 2). The first variable is superior migration of the
hip center compared to the obturator line. This indicates whether the acetabular
dome is intact. The second variable is the extent of teardrop destruction, which is
indicative of medial wall integrity. The third variable is the amount of ischial osteolysis.
Ischial bone destruction indicates loss of posterior wall integrity. The fourth variable is
an intact or a disrupted ilioischial line, which represents posterior column integrity.4

The important factor in evaluating acetabular bone stock is determining the ability to
use a hemispheric acetabular component alone with or without metal augments
versus the need to supplement with a cage or to plan for a custom triflange
component. 5 (Video 2). Other techniques, such as acetabular distraction, also are
viable options for patients with chronic pelvic discontinuity.6,7 Management is based
on the available bone (Video 3). Most acetabular revision procedures can be
performed with the use of a hemispheric acetabular component with or without
cancellous bone chips.

Paprosky classification system (surgical/prognostic; Figure 9)
Type I: minimal loss of metaphyseal bone and intact diaphysis (Figure 10)
Management: noncemented or cemented femoral implant
Type II: metaphyseal bone loss and intact diaphysis (Figure 11)
Management: extensively porous-coated or on-growth conical, tapered stem revision
component
Type IIIA: metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone loss with more than 4 cm of the diaphysis
intact (Figure 12)
Management: extensively porous-coated or on-growth conical, tapered stem
Type IIIB: metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone loss with less than 4 cm of the diaphysis intact
(Figure 13)
Management: conical tapered stem
Type IV: extensively deficient metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone
Management: proximal femur replacement; allograft-prosthetic composite
Impaction grafting techniques also may be used for procedures involving conical tapered
stems; however, they are infrequently used by most surgeons in North America.

Femur
On the femoral side, the Paprosky classification system is most used to describe bone
loss. This classification system is especially beneficial because it represents a
stepwise, algorithmic approach to femoral bone loss based on the reconstruction
options that are viable in each category. Therefore, bone loss is separated into
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:33 AM
AAOS | Bone Loss Classification: Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002011
19/22

metaphyseal and diaphyseal. If metaphyseal bone loss is minimal, the diaphyseal
bone usually remains intact, and primary type components often can be used. If
metaphyseal bone loss is substantial, the status of the diaphyseal bone dictates the
type of distal fixation that will be required. Historically, the demarcation between type
IIIA and type IIIB bone loss was associated with critical treatment ramifications
because fully porous-coated cylindrical stems could be reliably used in type IIIA but
not type IIIB bone defects. Currently, a conical fluted, tapered stem (nonmodular or
modular) commonly is used, and adequate distal fixation can be achieved for type IIIA
and type IIIB defects;8,9 however, more extensive megaprostheses may be necessary
as supportive diaphyseal bone decreases, as in type IV defects.10
